Well, yeah, absolutely it's on purpose. I mean, you don't just accidentally get this disciplined, right? It takes a lot of planning. When you work with heavy machinery, you learn pretty quick that precision is everything. You don't just wing it. You have to know exactly what you're doing at all times, and I just apply that same exact logic to myself. I have my routine completely dialed in now. 

Most days, I just keep it to coffee before the early shift—just black coffee, because it gets me going without making me feel all weighed down and sluggish while I'm trying to set up the presses. And then at lunch, while the rest of the crew is ordering these massive, greasy meals from the food trucks that just put them in a food coma by 2 PM, I'll have maybe half a protein bar. Just half. It's exactly enough fuel to keep the engine running, you know? And then when I clock out, I go home, I do some yoga to stretch out my back from standing on the concrete all day, and I'll just have a small bowl of vegetables after that. 

That's it. It's clean, it's efficient. Because honestly... if I start eating more than that, the whole day just feels completely out of control. Like I've lost my grip on the wheel. People look at me and they think I'm depriving myself, like those nurses at occupational health, but they don't understand how incredible it feels to just run on exactly what you need and absolutely nothing more. It's like calibrating a machine to run at peak performance. You don't just dump excess oil into a hydraulic system, you give it the exact specs it needs. If I let myself eat whatever, or eat more, I just... I can feel myself getting soft, losing that edge, losing that tightness, and I just can't let that happen. So yes, it's highly intentional, but it's about efficiency and focus, not whatever they think it is.

Well, it's not exactly about wanting to be *thinner*, per se, like I'm not looking in the mirror and trying to disappear. It's more about... it's about the maintenance of it all. The absolute terror of going backward. Because I've worked so incredibly hard to get this machine running exactly the way it is right now, to get this lean and this disciplined.

I can't go back to that. I absolutely cannot. So when you ask if I want to be thinner... I just want to be safe. I want to stay exactly where I am, or maybe just a little bit leaner, just as a buffer, you know? Well, yeah. I mean, yes, absolutely. It's... it's exactly what I was just saying about the scale. That's the whole thing, isn't it? It's not just a casual preference, it's this absolute, overwhelming fear that if I don't keep the intake strictly limited, if I don't measure everything down to the exact fraction, then I'm going to start gaining weight. And if the scale goes up even a little bit—like I said, even if it's just a quarter of a pound, which I know people say is just water weight or whatever, but to me, it's a warning light flashing on the dashboard. It means the system is failing. 

I just panic. I completely panic that I'm going to lose all the control I've worked so incredibly hard for. Because it takes so much effort to maintain this level of discipline. It's not easy to just have half a protein bar while everyone else is eating whatever they want, but I do it because the alternative is terrifying. The thought of ending up heavy again, of feeling that sluggishness creeping back in, of losing that edge on the factory floor... I can't let that happen. 

I remember a few years ago, before I really got my routine dialed in, I had this period where I was just eating normally, whatever that means, and I felt so slow. My joints ached after a 10-hour shift, my lower back was always killing me, and I just felt like this heavy, unmanageable block of lead. I hated it. I hated feeling out of control of my own body. So now, every single time I think about eating something extra, or having a full meal instead of just my usual, all I can see is that number on the scale creeping up. And I know if I give an inch, I'll take a mile, and before I know it, I'll be right back where I started. So yes, the limitation is entirely because I am terrified—just absolutely terrified—of gaining the weight back and losing the grip I finally have on myself.

Yes, I mean, like I was saying before, the fear of the scale going up is just paralyzing. But it’s also... it’s about how the day actually feels, you know? The structure of it. If I deviate even a little bit from my routine, my brain just completely short-circuits. So, to prevent that, to keep that fear at bay and keep everything running smoothly, I have this very, very specific schedule that I stick to. 

Most days, I just keep it to black coffee before the early shift. I have to be at the plant by 6 AM, so I’m up at 4:30, and I’ll just have that coffee while I’m getting ready and going over the production schedules in my head. It gives me enough energy to get the machines calibrated. Then, when the lunch whistle blows—and the break room is always so loud and chaotic, with all the guys eating these massive, heavy sandwiches and ordering takeout—I just can't be around it. I'll usually go sit in my car or find a quiet corner by the loading dock, and I’ll have maybe half a protein bar. Just half. I wrap the other half up perfectly in the foil for the next day. It's just enough to keep my hands steady for the afternoon work.

And then I finish my shift, deal with the presses and the heat, and after I clock out, I go straight to my yoga class to try and stretch out my lower back, because standing on that concrete floor all day really takes a toll on you. By the time I finally get home, I’ll just make myself a small bowl of vegetables. Usually just steamed broccoli or spinach, nothing added to it, no butter or oil or anything like that. And that’s it. That’s my entire day. 

I have to do it exactly like that because honestly, if I try to eat more than that... if someone brings donuts into the shop and I have one, or if I try to have a full meal in the evening... it’s not just the terror of the weight gain, though that is huge. It's that eating more makes the whole day feel completely out of control. Like the edges are fraying and the whole system I've built is just going to collapse on top of me. I start overthinking every single movement I make, wondering if I'm burning enough off, wondering if I ruined my progress. I just can't handle that kind of mental noise. So sticking to the coffee, the half bar, and the vegetables... it keeps the noise down. It keeps me safe.

Exactly. Yes, it’s exactly what I was just trying to explain to you. That routine—keeping it strictly to just the black coffee before my early shift, maybe that half of a protein bar at lunch, and then just the small bowl of plain vegetables after my yoga class... that is the glue. The routine—the coffee, the half bar, the vegetables—it's like... it's like the scaffolding holding my entire life up. Without it, I'm just chaos. Complete, unmanageable chaos.

They pulled me into the little side office and actually told me my weight is dangerously low. Dangerously low! They said it's a safety hazard for someone running presses and doing fabrication all day. But I just... I couldn't believe it, because I honestly thought I was just getting leaner. You know, more disciplined. I'm 45, and I've been really focusing on cutting out all the excess, just being incredibly strict with myself so I don't get sluggish on the line. I feel like I'm just finally getting my body under total control, and now they're threatening to pull me off my station, saying I'm too small or too fragile or something, which is just ridiculous because I feel lighter and more focused than I have in years. I mean, discipline is supposed to be a good thing, right? It takes a lot of willpower to stay this lean. But they just wouldn't listen, they just kept looking at the numbers on the scale and shaking their heads, and they basically forced me to come see you before they'll clear me to go back to my normal shift.\n\nDoctor: When you say you've been cutting out all the excess, is that something you're doing on purpose to control your weight?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, absolutely it's on purpose. I mean, you don't just accidentally get this disciplined, right? It takes a lot of planning. When you work with heavy machinery, you learn pretty quick that precision is everything. You don't just wing it. You have to know exactly what you're doing at all times, and I just apply that same exact logic to myself. I have my routine completely dialed in now. \n\nMost days, I just keep it to coffee before the early shift—just black coffee, because it gets me going without making me feel all weighed down and sluggish while I'm trying to set up the presses. And then at lunch, while the rest of the crew is ordering these massive, greasy meals from the food trucks that just put them in a food coma by 2 PM, I'll have maybe half a protein bar. Just half. It's exactly enough fuel to keep the engine running, you know? And then when I clock out, I go home, I do some yoga to stretch out my back from standing on the concrete all day, and I'll just have a small bowl of vegetables after that. \n\nThat's it. It's clean, it's efficient. Because honestly... if I start eating more than that, the whole day just feels completely out of control. Like I've lost my grip on the wheel. People look at me and they think I'm depriving myself, like those nurses at occupational health, but they don't understand how incredible it feels to just run on exactly what you need and absolutely nothing more. It's like calibrating a machine to run at peak performance. You don't just dump excess oil into a hydraulic system, you give it the exact specs it needs. If I let myself eat whatever, or eat more, I just... I can feel myself getting soft, losing that edge, losing that tightness, and I just can't let that happen. So yes, it's highly intentional, but it's about efficiency and focus, not whatever they think it is.\n\nDoctor: Do you want to be thinner than you are now?\n\nPatient: Well, it's not exactly about wanting to be *thinner*, per se, like I'm not looking in the mirror and trying to disappear. It's more about... it's about the maintenance of it all. The absolute terror of going backward. Because I've worked so incredibly hard to get this machine running exactly the way it is right now, to get this lean and this disciplined. \n\nAnd the thing is, I weigh myself every morning. Every single morning, right after I wake up, before I even have a sip of water, because you need the baseline to be consistent, right? And if I step on that scale and the number has gone up—even by just a fraction of a pound, even if it's just a tiny, tiny little blip—I just completely panic. I mean, my heart starts racing, my chest gets tight, and I just think, \"This is it. This is the moment I lose my grip.\" Because if it goes up a little today, what stops it from going up a little tomorrow? And the next day? And suddenly I'm spiraling, and I'm going to lose all of this control I've fought so hard for, and I'll just end up heavy and sluggish again, like I used to be. \n\nI remember how that felt, carrying around all that excess weight on the factory floor, feeling tired by noon, feeling like my body was just this heavy, unmanageable thing dragging me down. I can't go back to that. I absolutely cannot. So when you ask if I want to be thinner... I just want to be safe. I want to stay exactly where I am, or maybe just a little bit leaner, just as a buffer, you know? Just a tiny bit more of a safety margin so that if there is a fluctuation, I don't instantly tip over into losing everything. Because that panic, when the scale goes up... it just consumes my whole day. I can't focus on the presses, I can't focus on the schematics, all I can think about is how I have to tighten the reins even more to fix it.\n\nDoctor: Is your decision to limit your food intake mostly because you're afraid of gaining weight?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah. I mean, yes, absolutely. It's... it's exactly what I was just saying about the scale. That's the whole thing, isn't it? It's not just a casual preference, it's this absolute, overwhelming fear that if I don't keep the intake strictly limited, if I don't measure everything down to the exact fraction, then I'm going to start gaining weight. And if the scale goes up even a little bit—like I said, even if it's just a quarter of a pound, which I know people say is just water weight or whatever, but to me, it's a warning light flashing on the dashboard. It means the system is failing. \n\nI just panic. I completely panic that I'm going to lose all the control I've worked so incredibly hard for. Because it takes so much effort to maintain this level of discipline. It's not easy to just have half a protein bar while everyone else is eating whatever they want, but I do it because the alternative is terrifying. The thought of ending up heavy again, of feeling that sluggishness creeping back in, of losing that edge on the factory floor... I can't let that happen. \n\nI remember a few years ago, before I really got my routine dialed in, I had this period where I was just eating normally, whatever that means, and I felt so slow. My joints ached after a 10-hour shift, my lower back was always killing me, and I just felt like this heavy, unmanageable block of lead. I hated it. I hated feeling out of control of my own body. So now, every single time I think about eating something extra, or having a full meal instead of just my usual, all I can see is that number on the scale creeping up. And I know if I give an inch, I'll take a mile, and before I know it, I'll be right back where I started. So yes, the limitation is entirely because I am terrified—just absolutely terrified—of gaining the weight back and losing the grip I finally have on myself.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would look good if you weighed a bit more?\n\nPatient: Look good? God, no. No, no, no. I mean, I already struggle so much with how I look right now. If I weighed more, I think I'd completely lose my mind. Because, see, even right now, with everything I'm doing, with all the discipline and the strict routines... I still see so much wrong. \n\nWhen I walk past the big safety windows on the shop floor—you know, the ones that separate the heavy presses from the supervisor's office? They have this reflective tint to them so they basically act like mirrors when the overhead lights hit them right. Or even just when I go into the employee bathroom to wash the grease off my hands... I'll catch a glimpse of myself, and all I can see, the absolute *only* thing my eyes lock onto, is my stomach and my thighs. They just look so big to me. Too big. I'll just stand there at the sink in that awful, cheap fluorescent lighting, and I just stare at my stomach and my thighs, and I see all this... this bulk that just shouldn't be there. It doesn't look efficient. It looks wrong. \n\nAnd honestly, seeing that just completely ruins how I feel about myself for the rest of the entire day. It just derails me. I'll go back out to the floor and I can't even concentrate on the schematics properly because I'm just hyper-fixating on how my work pants are sitting on my legs, or how my stomach feels when I bend over to check a pressure gauge. It just eats away at me, this feeling of being too big, and it makes me feel disgusting, like I'm failing at everything. So if I weighed *more*? If there was even more of me catching the light in those reflections? Absolutely not. I'd never be able to look in a mirror again. I can barely stand what's there right now, so the idea of adding to it... no, I definitely wouldn't look good. I'd look terrible.\n\nDoctor: Is your fear of gaining weight the main reason you're being so strict with your eating?\n\nPatient: Yes, I mean, like I was saying before, the fear of the scale going up is just paralyzing. But it’s also... it’s about how the day actually feels, you know? The structure of it. If I deviate even a little bit from my routine, my brain just completely short-circuits. So, to prevent that, to keep that fear at bay and keep everything running smoothly, I have this very, very specific schedule that I stick to. \n\nMost days, I just keep it to black coffee before the early shift. I have to be at the plant by 6 AM, so I’m up at 4:30, and I’ll just have that coffee while I’m getting ready and going over the production schedules in my head. It gives me enough energy to get the machines calibrated. Then, when the lunch whistle blows—and the break room is always so loud and chaotic, with all the guys eating these massive, heavy sandwiches and ordering takeout—I just can't be around it. I'll usually go sit in my car or find a quiet corner by the loading dock, and I’ll have maybe half a protein bar. Just half. I wrap the other half up perfectly in the foil for the next day. It's just enough to keep my hands steady for the afternoon work.\n\nAnd then I finish my shift, deal with the presses and the heat, and after I clock out, I go straight to my yoga class to try and stretch out my lower back, because standing on that concrete floor all day really takes a toll on you. By the time I finally get home, I’ll just make myself a small bowl of vegetables. Usually just steamed broccoli or spinach, nothing added to it, no butter or oil or anything like that. And that’s it. That’s my entire day. \n\nI have to do it exactly like that because honestly, if I try to eat more than that... if someone brings donuts into the shop and I have one, or if I try to have a full meal in the evening... it’s not just the terror of the weight gain, though that is huge.
